content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published guidance for the transport of infectious substances for the years 2023–2024. This document is available in both electronic and print formats, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-008952-5 and 978-92-4-008953-2. The original English version remains the binding and authentic edition. The guidance provides practical instructions to ensure compliance with international regulations for the transport of infectious substances across all modes of transport. It includes updates effective from October 1, 2023, and outlines frameworks for classifying, identifying, packaging, marking, labeling, documenting, and refrigerating infectious substances to ensure their safe delivery. The document targets all stakeholders involved in the shipping process, including shippers, packaging suppliers, carriers, and receivers. This edition replaces the 2021 version and reflects updates from source documents. It is connected to WHO activities such as biosafety and biosecurity training and the Infectious Substances Shipping Training (ISST). The guidance emphasizes the importance of adhering to national and international regulations when handling potentially hazardous biological materials. The document acknowledges contributions from WHO staff and external experts, including Lisa Stevens, Rica Zinsky, Markus Huber, Monika Gsell Albert, and Katherine Rooney. The production and technical editing were led by Kazunobu Kojima. The guidance highlights the critical role of international regulations in ensuring the safe transport of infectious substances. Facilities handling biological agents must ensure proper identification, storage, and control of these agents in accordance with best practices. During transport, there is a risk of exposure to people and the environment, which necessitates strict adherence to international recommendations and regulations. The UN Model Regulations, developed by the UN Committee of Experts on the Transport of Dangerous Goods (UNCETDG), provide a widely recognized framework for the safe transport of dangerous goods, including infectious substances. These regulations are reviewed biennially to incorporate technical advancements, new materials, and emerging safety requirements. They aim to harmonize transport provisions across national and international regulations while allowing flexibility for local adaptations. Various international modal agreements, such as the ICAO Technical Instructions for air transport, RID for rail transport, ADR for road transport, and the IMDG Code for sea transport, adapt the UN Model Regulations for specific modes of transport. These agreements are legally binding and regularly updated to reflect new safety requirements. For postal services, the Universal Postal Union (UPU) uses the ICAO Technical Instructions as a basis for shipments, although high-risk infectious substances (Category A) are not accepted. Regional and subregional regulations, such as those in the European Union, address specific elements like the transport of animal by-products and pathogens to minimize the risk of disease transmission. Standardized labeling systems, such as Hazchem, are used in regions like Southeast Asia and Australia to ensure consistent communication of hazardous chemical information. National regulations often adopt the UN Model Regulations or their modal agreements, with variations to suit local conditions. National authorities are responsible for providing details of their requirements to users. In the absence of national regulations, international agreements serve as the default standard.
